extracted.intended_audience: literate 19th-century travelers and readers of literary travel letters / cultural commentary
extracted.subtask_description: First‑person travel letters and cultural commentary recounting visits to Paris, Italy, and other European locales, mixing aesthetic judgements, social criticism, and institutional observations. These are episodic travel-essays intended for a general educated readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opera singer appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations of singers emphasize qualities like charm of voice, grace, tenderness, range of power, talent, good taste, and personal beauty; singers should 'fill their parts' and also ideally exhibit a higher inspiration ('a ray of the Muse').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete indicators: voice charm and timbre, expressive grace and tenderness, sufficient vocal range and power for the role, technical talent and musical taste, stage presence/personal beauty, and the presence of inspiration beyond mere competence. Anti-pattern: performers who 'fill their parts' adequately yet lack any inspiring artistic spark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music performance authenticity (composer-as-performer)
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'feel' the true merits of certain music (e.g., Chopin) one must hear the composer himself; imperfect performers obscure subtle secrets of the creative spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference is given to hearing the original/composer or performers who can authentically convey the composer's subtleties. Anti-patterns: hearing only imperfect or second‑rate performances that fail to transmit the work's essential character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Good oratory is judged by a combination of logic, plausibility, rapidity, occasional fiery bursts, polish, force and scope, dignity, and 'inward strength' rather than mere cultivated intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess speeches for coherence (logic), persuasive plausibility, rhetorical energy (pace, bursts), polish and craft, substantive force and breadth of vision, and personal authority/dignity. Example contrast: M. Berryer is 'not logical, but plausible, full and rapid' whereas Guizot's manner lacks dignity and inward strength. Weak oratory may have cultivated form but little moral or intellectual weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative speech engagement (commanding interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful speech in an assembly must 'command interest' — otherwise the audience reacts with impatience; dull, windily repetitive speeches are punished by the assembly's vivacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures of success: ability to hold attention, to present material that is new or instructive (not mere newspaper truism), and to provoke appropriate public feeling. Anti-patterns: long, clumsy reiterations of common press assertions that waste the assembly's time and provoke restlessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of books for international exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: International exchanges (e.g., M. Vattemare's project) should not send 'a great quantity of documents of merely local interest' but instead a curated selection that is 'honorable to us and of value to the French' — items on commerce, manufactures, Congress proceedings, and materials illuminating aborigines are desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use persons of ability to make selections; prioritize materials of broad informational or scholarly value (commerce, industry, national institutions, indigenous history) rather than local ephemera. For lasting benefit, use accredited agents on both sides to manage exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evening schools for working classes (Frères Chrétiens) — success criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Evening lessons for working adults should produce surprising progress in reading and writing and especially in practical arts like drawing; such schools give working men access to the glories of art and science and to the refinements of home life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate by measurable improvements in literacy and drawing, the quality of student work (copies of good models), and by the extent to which the instruction enhances participants' dignity, taste, and domestic life. Institutional virtues: accessibility to workers, disinterested (non-commercial) service, and practical pedagogies that fit adult learners. Recommendation: create similar associations without overly priestly formality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charitable nursing/refuge institutions (Deaconesses / 'Home')
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective charitable institutions take sick children of the poor and nurse them until well and provide refuges for unjustly treated classes; they should show enlightened spirit rather than formal, ignorant treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria include practical healthcare (nursing until recovery), refuges that restore peace and usefulness, respect for human nature, and an enlightened, humane ethos. Anti-pattern: institutions that are 'too formal' and whose treatment shows ignorance of human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education for the intellectually disabled (School for 'Idiots')
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional programs for persons with severe cognitive impairments show success through gains in singing, gymnastic discipline, recitation, writing, drawing, vocational skills (shoemaking, carpentry), and in some cases surprising cognitive gains (e.g., mathematical aptitude unlocking reason).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate progress by concrete behaviors and skills (memory, recitation, musicality, manual trades, sensory discrimination). Emphasize patience, individualized attention, early intervention when possible, and vocational as well as artistic training. Case example: a formerly brutalized boy made measurable gains through mathematics and patient care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Childcare for industrial workers (crèches and wet-nurses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed crèches should not merely keep children by day but provide wet-nurses and supervised care so infants receive nourishment from healthier persons, preserving mother–child bonds while preventing degeneration (and countering harmful local practices like feeding children opium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features: on‑site daytime care, provision of healthy nursing, supervision by directors, allowance for maternal visits, and aiming to prevent physical and social deterioration. Intended outcomes: healthier children, reduced maternal burden, preserved family ties, and improved long‑term population health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public festivals and social awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Public pageants or processions (e.g., 'the procession of the Fat Ox') risk being a sham when the populace is suffering; civic celebrations should not hide or ignore the hunger and destitution experienced by poorer classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good public ceremony should reflect social reality and avoid masking widespread suffering. Anti-patterns: suppression of critical pamphlets ('The Voice of Famine') and a festival that feigns plenty while ignoring hunger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel writing — convey feeling, not just sight
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid travel impression is not merely visual description ('I saw how beautiful they were') but the felt, experiential reaction; good travel writing should make the reader feel, not only see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer passages that communicate emotional and sensory experience (mood, atmosphere, inward reaction) over detached catalogues of sights. Anti-pattern: purely ocular descriptions that fail to convey personal engagement or affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural centres as pedagogical resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites like Paris are valuable because they contain 'abundance of teachers who could bear being examined by the pupil' — cultural centres should enable rigorous inquiry and ready access to expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure a cultural centre by the openness and competence of its teachers, the availability of experts who will be interrogated by learners, and the breadth of accessible knowledge. Anti-pattern: places where experience or local knowledge is inaccessible to earnest inquiry.
